Proof To prove uniqueness, let  $E$  be a map with the properties stated. Let  $\theta = (n,\theta)$  be an object of  $FP$ ; thus,  $n \geq 0$  and  $\theta \in P_n$ . By definition of the categorical  $P$ -algebra structure on  $FP$ ,

$$
\theta = \bar {\theta} (1 _ {P}, \dots , 1 _ {P}).
$$

Applying  $E$  to both sides gives

$$
E (\theta) = E \left(\bar {\theta} \left(1 _ {P}, \dots , 1 _ {P}\right)\right) = \bar {\theta} \left(E \left(1 _ {P}\right), \dots , E \left(1 _ {P}\right)\right) = \bar {\theta} (a, \dots , a),
$$

where the second equality holds because  $E$  is a strict map of categorical  $P$ -algebras, and the last is by hypothesis. Hence

$$
E (\theta) = \bar {\theta} (a, \dots , a), \tag {12.13}
$$

which determines  $E$  uniquely on the objects of  $FP$ .

To show the same for maps, take a map

$$
\langle \phi^ {1}, \dots , \phi^ {n} \rangle_ {\theta} \colon \psi \rightarrow \theta
$$

in  $FP$ . By Lemma 12.4.2(ii),

$$
\langle \phi^ {1}, \dots , \phi^ {n} \rangle_ {\theta} = \bar {\theta} \left(! _ {\phi^ {1}}, \dots ,!,! _ {\phi^ {n}}\right).
$$

Applying  $E$  to both sides gives

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \left(\left\langle \phi^ {1}, \dots , \phi^ {n} \right\rangle_ {\theta}\right) = E \left(\bar {\theta} \left(! _ {\phi^ {1}}, \dots , ! _ {\phi^ {n}}\right)\right) \\ = \bar {\theta} \left(E \left(\left. \begin{array}{l} \phi^ {1} \end{array} \right.\right), \dots , E \left(\left. \begin{array}{l} \phi^ {n} \end{array} \right.\right)\right) \\ = \bar {\theta} \left(\gamma_ {\phi^ {1}}, \dots , \gamma_ {\phi^ {n}}\right), \\ \end{array}
$$

for the same reasons as in the argument for objects. Hence

$$
E \left(\left\langle \phi^ {1}, \dots , \phi^ {n} \right\rangle_ {\theta}\right) = \bar {\theta} \left(\gamma_ {\phi^ {1}}, \dots , \gamma_ {\phi^ {n}}\right), \tag {12.14}
$$

which determines  $E$  uniquely on the maps in  $FP$ . We have therefore proved uniqueness.

To prove existence, we define  $E$  on objects by equation (12.13) and on maps by equation (12.14). Verifying that  $E$  satisfies the stated conditions (including continuity in the topological case) is a series of routine checks.

Corollary 12.4.7 Let  $P$  be an operad of sets or topological spaces. Let  $\mathbf{A}$  be a categorical  $P$ -algebra. Then there is a canonical bijection between internal algebras in  $\mathbf{A}$  and strict maps  $FP \to \mathbf{A}$  of categorical  $P$ -algebras.

Thus, an internal algebra in  $\mathbf{A}$  can be described as either a lax map  $\mathbf{1} \to \mathbf{A}$  or a strict map  $FP \to \mathbf{A}$ .

Example 12.4.8 In the case  $P = \mathbf{1}$ , Theorem 12.4.6 states that for any strict monoidal category  $\mathbf{A}$  and monoid  $a$  in  $\mathbf{A}$ , there is exactly one strict monoidal functor  $E: \mathbf{D} \to \mathbf{A}$  that maps the trivial monoid 1 in  $\mathbf{D}$  to the given monoid  $a$  in  $\mathbf{A}$ .

Hence, Corollary 12.4.7 implies that given just a monoidal category  $\mathbf{A}$ , the monoids in  $\mathbf{A}$  correspond naturally to the strict monoidal functors  $\mathbf{D} \to \mathbf{A}$ . We have therefore recovered the classical fact that a monoid in  $\mathbf{A}$  can be described as either a lax monoidal functor  $\mathbf{1} \to \mathbf{A}$  or a strict monoidal functor  $\mathbf{D} \to \mathbf{A}$  (paragraph (5.4.1) of Bénabou [34] and Proposition VII.5.1 of Mac Lane [234], for instance).

Now consider Theorem 12.4.6 in the case where  $P$  is the topological operad  $\Delta$  and  $\mathbf{A}$  is the topological monoid  $\mathbb{R}$ . By Corollary 12.4.7, the strict maps  $F\Delta \to \mathbf{A}$  of categorical  $\Delta$ -algebras are in natural bijection with the internal  $\Delta$ -algebras in  $\mathbf{A}$ . By Theorem 12.3.1, these in turn correspond to real scalar multiples of Shannon entropy. Together, these results imply that the strict maps  $F\Delta \to \mathbf{A}$  are naturally parametrized by  $\mathbb{R}$ .

We now make this parametrization explicit. Since  $\mathbf{A}$  has only one object, a strict map  $F\Delta \to \mathbf{A}$  of categorical  $\Delta$ -algebras amounts to a function

$$
E \colon \{\text {m a p s i n} F \Delta \} \rightarrow \mathbb {R}
$$

satisfying certain conditions. Our final theorem classifies such functions.

Theorem 12.4.9 Let  $E$  be a function  $\{\text{maps in } F\Delta \} \to \mathbb{R}$ . The following are equivalent:

i.  $E$  defines a strict map  $F\Delta \to \mathbb{R}$  of categorical  $\Delta$ -algebras in  $\mathbf{Top}$  (with respect to the standard categorical  $\Delta$ -algebra structure on  $\mathbb{R}$ );

ii. there is some  $c \in \mathbb{R}$  such that for all maps  $f: \mathbf{s} \to \mathbf{p}$  in  $F\Delta$

$$
E (f) = c \left(H (\mathbf {s}) - H (\mathbf {p})\right).
$$

Proof First assume (i). Applying  $E$  to the internal algebra  $(\mathbf{u}_1, !)$  in  $F\Delta$  gives an internal algebra  $E(\mathbf{u}_1, !)$  in  $\mathbb{R}$  (whose underlying object is necessarily the unique object of the category  $\mathbb{R}$ ). So by Theorem 12.3.1, there is some constant  $c \in \mathbb{R}$  such that  $E(!_{\mathbf{p}}) = cH(\mathbf{p})$  for all  $n \geq 1$  and  $\mathbf{p} \in \Delta_n$ .

Now take any map

$$
\langle \mathbf {r} ^ {1}, \dots , \mathbf {r} ^ {n} \rangle_ {\mathbf {p}}: \mathbf {s} \rightarrow \mathbf {p} \tag {12.15}
$$

in  $F\Delta$ . Since  $\mathbf{u}_1$  is terminal in  $F\Delta$ , there is a commutative triangle

![](images/6d34c151adf1b9078ef5107733840863f8bc44de6ccb06ad9bbd19ac957b2c9b.jpg)

in  $F\Delta$ . Applying the functor  $E$  to this triangle gives

$$
E \left(\left! \mathbf {s}\right)\left. \right) = E \left(\left! \mathbf {p}\right)\left. \right) + E \left(\left\langle \mathbf {r} ^ {1}, \dots , \mathbf {r} ^ {n} \right\rangle_ {\mathbf {p}}\right), \tag {12.17}
$$

which by the result of the last paragraph gives

$$
c H (\mathbf {s}) = c H (\mathbf {p}) + E \left(\left\langle \mathbf {r} ^ {1}, \dots , \mathbf {r} ^ {n} \right\rangle_ {\mathbf {p}}\right),
$$

proving (ii).

To show that (ii) implies (i), let  $c \in \mathbb{R}$ . By Theorem 12.3.1,  $cH$  defines an internal algebra structure on the unique object of the category  $\mathbb{R}$ . Now take a map (12.15) in  $F\Delta$ . By definition of  $E$ ,

$$
E \left(\left\langle \mathbf {r} ^ {1}, \dots , \mathbf {r} ^ {n} \right\rangle_ {\mathbf {p}}\right) = c \left(H (\mathbf {s}) - H (\mathbf {p})\right).
$$

But  $\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{p}\circ (\mathbf{r}^1,\dots ,\mathbf{r}^n)$  by definition of the maps in  $F\Delta$ , so by the chain rule,

$$
E \left(\left\langle \mathbf {r} ^ {1}, \dots , \mathbf {r} ^ {n} \right\rangle_ {\mathbf {p}}\right) = c \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} H (\mathbf {r} ^ {i}) = \bar {\mathbf {p}} \left(c H \left(\mathbf {r} ^ {1}\right), \dots , c H \left(\mathbf {r} ^ {n}\right)\right).
$$

It follows from the proof of Theorem 12.4.6 that  $E$  is a strict map  $F\Delta \to \mathbb{R}$  of categorical  $\Delta$ -algebras.

A result similar to Theorem 12.4.9 can also be proved for the  $q$ -logarithmic entropies, using the  $q$ -deformed categorical  $\Delta$ -algebra structure on  $\mathbb{R}$  and Theorem 12.3.2.

Theorem 12.4.9 bears a striking resemblance to the characterization of information loss in Theorem 10.2.1. It states that the strict maps  $F\Delta \to \mathbb{R}$  are the scalar multiples of the information loss function. But where one theorem uses the category  $F\Delta$ , the other uses the category FinProb of finite probability spaces. The explicit description of  $F\Delta$  in Example 12.4.4(iii) shows that there are three differences between  $F\Delta$  and FinProb. First, the maps in  $F\Delta$  are required to be order-preserving, whereas in FinProb there is no notion of ordering at all. Second, the category  $F\Delta$  is skeletal (isomorphic objects are equal), but FinProb is not. Third, the maps in the category  $F\Delta$  are not merely measure-preserving maps; they also come equipped with a probability distribution on the fibre over each zero-probability element of the codomain.

There is an analogue of Theorem 12.4.9 that comes close to Theorem 10.2.1; we sketch it now. It uses symmetric operads. As indicated in Remark 12.1.6(ii), a symmetric operad is an operad  $P$  together with an action of the symmetric group  $S_{n}$  on  $P_{n}$  for each  $n \geq 0$ , satisfying suitable axioms. For example, if  $A$  is an object of a symmetric monoidal category then the operad  $\operatorname{End}(A)$  of Example 12.1.2(v) has the structure of a symmetric operad. The operad  $\Delta$  is also symmetric in a natural way.

At the cost of some further complications, the notions of categorical  $P$ -algebra and internal algebra, and the construction of the free categorical  $P$ -algebra on an internal algebra, can be extended to symmetric operads  $P$ . The free categorical  $\Delta$ -algebra  $F_{\mathrm{sym}}\Delta$  on an internal algebra is much like  $F\Delta$ , but the maps are no longer required to be order-preserving. In other words, the first of the three differences between  $F\Delta$  and FinProb vanishes for  $F_{\mathrm{sym}}\Delta$ . The second, skeletality, is categorically unimportant. So, the only substantial difference between  $F_{\mathrm{sym}}\Delta$  and FinProb is the third: a map in  $F_{\mathrm{sym}}\Delta$  between finite probability spaces is a measure-preserving map together with a probability distribution on each fibre over an element of probability zero.

The symmetric analogue of Theorem 12.4.9 states that the strict maps  $F_{\mathrm{sym}} \Delta \to \mathbb{R}$  of symmetric categorical  $\Delta$ -algebras are precisely the scalar multiples of information loss. Translated into explicit terms, this theorem is nearly the same as the characterization of information loss in Theorem 10.2.1. The only difference is in the handling of zero probabilities. But the result can easily be adapted in an ad hoc way to discard the extra data associated with elements of probability zero, and it then becomes exactly Theorem 10.2.1. Historically, this categorical argument was, in fact, how the wholly elementary and concrete Theorem 10.2.1 was first obtained.

# Appendix A

# Proofs of background facts

This appendix consists of proofs deferred from the main text.

# A.1 Forms of the chain rule for entropy

In Remark 2.2.11, it was asserted that although the chain rule

$$
H \left(\mathbf {w} \circ \left(\mathbf {p} ^ {1}, \dots , \mathbf {p} ^ {n}\right)\right) = H (\mathbf {w}) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} w _ {i} H \left(\mathbf {p} ^ {i}\right)
$$

for Shannon entropy appears to be more general (that is, stronger) than the versions used by some previous authors, straightforward inductive arguments show that it is equivalent to those special cases. Remark 4.1.6 made a similar assertion for the  $q$ -logarithmic entropies  $S_{q}$ , where the equation becomes

$$
S _ {q} \left(\mathbf {w} \circ \left(\mathbf {p} ^ {1}, \dots , \mathbf {p} ^ {n}\right)\right) = S _ {q} (\mathbf {w}) + \sum_ {i \in \operatorname {s u p p} (\mathbf {w})} w _ {i} ^ {q} S _ {q} \left(\mathbf {p} ^ {i}\right).
$$

Here we prove those claims.

In Lemma A.1.1 below, part (i) is the general form of the chain rule, parts (ii) and (iv) are the special cases used by other authors, and part (iii) is an intermediate case that is helpful for the proof. Each of the four parts corresponds to a certain type of composition of probability distributions, depicted as a tree in Figure A.1.

Rather than working with sums over the support of  $\mathbf{w}$ , in this lemma we adopt the convention that  $0^q = 0$  for all  $q \in \mathbb{R}$ .

Lemma A.1.1 Let  $q \in \mathbb{R}$ . Let  $(I: \Delta_n \to \mathbb{R})_{n \geq 1}$  be a sequence of symmetric functions. The following are equivalent:

![](images/9a1f2a5156dd0e279258346ba3f76505ca2cc7d341a4bd1a798a8f96d045a037.jpg)

![](images/5bb2931854cc644f2037b91ca0552c52b79f49e1a1352802053fa04fcdd23f53.jpg)

![](images/f78bf620b85aec3e44d0dd911c837b51cece0d88026c193e3e990b613a82aa42.jpg)  
Figure A.1 Shapes of composites used in the four parts of Lemma A.1.1.

![](images/a0dc3683e893202e2220da04106b7b9113c4675ef13a581734ce714c5a9c2973.jpg)

i. for all  $n, k_1, \ldots, k_n \geq 1$ ,  $\mathbf{w} \in \Delta_n$ , and  $\mathbf{p}^i \in \Delta_{k_i}$

$$
I \left(\mathbf {w} \circ \left(\mathbf {p} ^ {1}, \dots , \mathbf {p} ^ {n}\right)\right) = I (\mathbf {w}) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} w _ {i} ^ {q} I \left(\mathbf {p} ^ {i}\right);
$$

ii. for all  $n \geq 1$ ,  $\mathbf{w} \in \Delta_n$ , and  $p \in [0,1]$

$$
I \left(w _ {1} p, w _ {1} (1 - p), w _ {2}, \dots , w _ {n}\right) = I (\mathbf {w}) + w _ {1} ^ {q} I (p, 1 - p);
$$

iii. for all  $n, k \geq 1$ ,  $\mathbf{w} \in \Delta_n$ , and  $\mathbf{p} \in \Delta_k$

$$
I \left(w _ {1} p _ {1}, \dots , w _ {1} p _ {k}, w _ {2}, \dots , w _ {n}\right) = I (\mathbf {w}) + w _ {1} ^ {q} I (\mathbf {p});
$$

iv. for all  $k,\ell \geq 1$ $\mathbf{p}\in \Delta_k$ $\mathbf{r}\in \Delta_{\ell}$  , and  $w\in [0,1]$

$$
\begin{array}{l} I (w p _ {1}, \dots , w p _ {k}, (1 - w) r _ {1}, \dots , (1 - w) r _ {\ell}) \\ = I (w, 1 - w) + w ^ {q} I (\mathbf {p}) + (1 - w) ^ {q} I (\mathbf {r}). \\ \end{array}
$$

Much of the following argument goes back to Feinstein ([97], p. 5-6).

Proof Trivially, (i) implies (ii).

Assuming (ii), we prove (iii) by induction on  $k$ . The case  $k = 1$  reduces to the statement that  $I(\mathbf{u}_1) = 0$ , which follows by taking  $n = 1$  in (ii). Now let  $k \geq 2$ , and assume the result for  $k - 1$ .

Let  $n \geq 1$ ,  $\mathbf{w} \in \Delta_n$ , and  $\mathbf{p} \in \Delta_k$ . By symmetry, we can assume that  $p_k < 1$ . Using the inductive hypothesis, we have

$$
\begin{array}{l} I (w _ {1} p _ {1}, \dots , w _ {1} p _ {k}, w _ {2}, \dots , w _ {n}) \\ = I \left(w _ {1} (1 - p _ {k}) \cdot \frac {p _ {1}}{1 - p _ {k}}, \dots , w _ {1} (1 - p _ {k}) \cdot \frac {p _ {k - 1}}{1 - p _ {k}}, w _ {1} p _ {k}, w _ {2}, \dots , w _ {n}\right) \\ = I \left(w _ {1} \left(1 - p _ {k}\right), w _ {1} p _ {k}, w _ {2}, \dots , w _ {n}\right) + \left(w _ {1} \left(1 - p _ {k}\right)\right) ^ {q} I \left(\frac {p _ {1}}{1 - p _ {k}}, \dots , \frac {p _ {k - 1}}{1 - p _ {k}}\right), \\ \end{array}
$$

which by (ii) is equal to

$$
I (\mathbf {w}) + w _ {1} ^ {q} \Bigg \{I (1 - p _ {k}, p _ {k}) + (1 - p _ {k}) ^ {q} I \Big (\frac {p _ {1}}{1 - p _ {k}}, \dots , \frac {p _ {k - 1}}{1 - p _ {k}} \Big) \Bigg \}.
$$

But by the inductive hypothesis again, the term  $\{\cdot \cdot \}$  is equal to

$$
I \left((1 - p _ {k}) \cdot \frac {p _ {1}}{1 - p _ {k}}, \dots , (1 - p _ {k}) \cdot \frac {p _ {k - 1}}{1 - p _ {k}}, p _ {k}\right) = I (\mathbf {p}),
$$

completing the induction.

Now assuming (iii), we prove (iv). Let  $k, \ell \geq 1$ ,  $\mathbf{p} \in \Delta_k$ ,  $\mathbf{r} \in \Delta_\ell$ , and  $w \in [0,1]$ . Using (iii), we have

$$
\begin{array}{l} I (w p _ {1}, \dots , w p _ {k}, (1 - w) r _ {1}, \dots , (1 - w) r _ {\ell}) \\ = I (w, (1 - w) r _ {1}, \dots , (1 - w) r _ {\ell}) + w ^ {q} I (\mathbf {p}). \\ \end{array}
$$

By symmetry and (iii) again, this in turn is equal to

$$
I (w, 1 - w) + (1 - w) ^ {q} I (\mathbf {r}) + w ^ {q} I (\mathbf {p}),
$$

proving (iv).

Finally, assume (iv). We prove (i) by induction on  $n$ . The case  $n = 1$  just states that  $I(\mathbf{u}_1) = 0$ , which follows from (iv) by taking  $k = \ell = 1$ . Now let  $n \geq 2$ , and assume the result for  $n - 1$ .

Let  $k_{1},\ldots ,k_{n}\geq 1$ $\mathbf{w}\in \Delta_n$  , and  $\mathbf{p}^i\in \Delta_{k_i}$  . By symmetry, we can assume that  $w_{1} > 0$  . Write

$$
\mathbf {p} ^ {1 2} = \left(\frac {w _ {1}}{w _ {1} + w _ {2}} p _ {1} ^ {1}, \dots , \frac {w _ {1}}{w _ {1} + w _ {2}} p _ {k _ {1}} ^ {1}, \frac {w _ {2}}{w _ {1} + w _ {2}} p _ {1} ^ {2}, \dots , \frac {w _ {2}}{w _ {1} + w _ {2}} p _ {k _ {2}} ^ {2}\right) \in \Delta_ {k _ {1} + k _ {2}}.
$$

Then

$$
\mathbf {w} \circ (\mathbf {p} ^ {1}, \ldots , \mathbf {p} ^ {n}) = (w _ {1} + w _ {2}, w _ {3}, \ldots , w _ {n}) \circ (\mathbf {p} ^ {1 2}, \mathbf {p} ^ {3}, \ldots , \mathbf {p} ^ {n}),
$$

so by inductive hypothesis,

$$
\begin{array}{l} I (\mathbf {w} \circ (\mathbf {p} ^ {1}, \dots , \mathbf {p} ^ {n})) \\ = I \left(w _ {1} + w _ {2}, w _ {3}, \dots , w _ {n}\right) + \left(w _ {1} + w _ {2}\right) ^ {q} I \left(\mathbf {p} ^ {1 2}\right) + \sum_ {i = 3} ^ {n} w _ {i} ^ {q} I \left(\mathbf {p} ^ {i}\right). \tag {A.1} \\ \end{array}
$$

On the other hand, by (iv),

$$
I (\mathbf {p} ^ {1 2}) = I \left(\frac {w _ {1}}{w _ {1} + w _ {2}}, \frac {w _ {2}}{w _ {1} + w _ {2}}\right) + \left(\frac {w _ {1}}{w _ {1} + w _ {2}}\right) ^ {q} I (\mathbf {p} ^ {1}) + \left(\frac {w _ {2}}{w _ {1} + w _ {2}}\right) ^ {q} I (\mathbf {p} ^ {2}).
$$

Substituting this into (A.1), we deduce that  $I(\mathbf{w} \circ (\mathbf{p}^1, \dots, \mathbf{p}^n))$  is equal to

$$
I \left(w _ {1} + w _ {2}, w _ {3}, \dots , w _ {n}\right) + \left(w _ {1} + w _ {2}\right) ^ {q} I \left(\frac {w _ {1}}{w _ {1} + w _ {2}}, \frac {w _ {2}}{w _ {1} + w _ {2}}\right) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} w _ {i} ^ {q} I \left(\mathbf {p} ^ {i}\right). \tag {A.2}
$$

But applying the inductive hypothesis to the composite

$$
\mathbf {w} = \left(w _ {1} + w _ {2}, w _ {3}, \dots , w _ {n}\right) \circ \left(\left(\frac {w _ {1}}{w _ {1} + w _ {2}}, \frac {w _ {2}}{w _ {1} + w _ {2}}\right), \mathbf {u} _ {1}, \dots , \mathbf {u} _ {1}\right)
$$

gives

$$
I (\mathbf {w}) = I \left(w _ {1} + w _ {2}, w _ {3}, \dots , w _ {n}\right) + \left(w _ {1} + w _ {2}\right) ^ {q} I \left(\frac {w _ {1}}{w _ {1} + w _ {2}}, \frac {w _ {2}}{w _ {1} + w _ {2}}\right)
$$

(recalling that  $I(\mathbf{u}_1) = 0$ ). Hence the expression (A.2) reduces to

$$
I (\mathbf {w}) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} w _ {i} ^ {q} I (\mathbf {p} ^ {i}),
$$

proving (i).

# A.2 The expected number of species in a random sample

Here we prove the result stated in Example 4.3.6, which expresses the diversity index of Hurlbert, Smith and Grassle in terms of the Hill numbers  $D_{q}(\mathbf{p})$ .

Recall that we are modelling an ecological community with  $n$  species via its relative abundance distribution, and that  $H_{m}^{\mathrm{HSG}}(\mathbf{p})$  denotes the expected number of different species represented in a random sample with replacement of  $m$  individuals. The claim is that

$$
H _ {m} ^ {\mathrm {H S G}} (\mathbf {p}) = \sum_ {q = 1} ^ {m} (- 1) ^ {q - 1} \binom {m} {q} D _ {q} (\mathbf {p}) ^ {1 - q}.
$$

Define random variables  $X_{1},\ldots ,X_{n}$  by

$$
X _ {i} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \text {i f s p e c i e s i i s p r e s e n t i n t h e s a m p l e ,} \\ 0 & \text {o t h e r w i s e .} \end{array} \right.
$$

Then  $\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i}$  is the number of different species in the sample, so

$$
\begin{array}{l} H _ {m} ^ {\mathrm {H S G}} (\mathbf {p}) = \mathbb {E} \left(\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} X _ {i}\right) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mathbb {E} (X _ {i}) \\ = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mathbb {P} (\text {s p e c i e s} i \text {i s p r e s e n t i n t h e s a m p l e}) \\ = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \left(1 - \left(1 - p _ {i}\right) ^ {m}\right), \\ \end{array}
$$

as Hurlbert observed (equation (14) of [148]). It follows that

$$
\begin{array}{l} H _ {m} ^ {\mathrm {H S G}} (\mathbf {p}) = n - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {q = 0} ^ {m} \binom {m} {q} (- p _ {i}) ^ {q} \\ = n - \sum_ {q = 0} ^ {m} (- 1) ^ {q} \binom {m} {q} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} ^ {q} \\ = n - \left\{\binom {m} {0} n - \binom {m} {1} 1 + \sum_ {q = 2} ^ {m} (- 1) ^ {q} \binom {m} {q} D _ {q} (\mathbf {p}) ^ {1 - q} \right\} \\ = m - \sum_ {q = 2} ^ {m} (- 1) ^ {q} \binom {m} {q} D _ {q} (\mathbf {p}) ^ {1 - q} \\ = \sum_ {q = 1} ^ {m} (- 1) ^ {q - 1} \binom {m} {q} D _ {q} (\mathbf {p}) ^ {1 - q}, \\ \end{array}
$$

as claimed.

# A.3 The diversity profile determines the distribution

Here we prove the result claimed in Remark 4.4.9: two probability distributions on the same finite set have the same diversity profile if and only if one is a permutation of the other. Formally:

Lemma A.3.1 Let  $n \geq 1$  and  $\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{r} \in \Delta_n$ . The following are equivalent:

i.  $D_{q}(\mathbf{p}) = D_{q}(\mathbf{r})$  for all  $q\in [-\infty ,\infty ]$

ii. there exists a subset  $Q \subseteq [-\infty, \infty)$ , unbounded above, such that  $D_q(\mathbf{p}) = D_q(\mathbf{r})$  for all  $q \in Q$ ;

iii.  $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r}\sigma$  for some permutation  $\sigma$  of  $\{1,\ldots ,n\}$

This result first appeared as Proposition A22 of the appendix to Leinster and Cobbold [218].

Proof (iii) implies (i) by the symmetry of the Hill numbers (Lemma 4.4.8), and (i) implies (ii) trivially. Now assuming (ii), we prove (iii) by induction on  $n$ . It is trivial for  $n = 1$ . Let  $n \geq 2$ , assume the result for  $n - 1$ , and take  $\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{r} \in \Delta_n$  such that  $D_q(\mathbf{p}) = D_q(\mathbf{r})$  for all elements  $q$  of some set  $Q \subseteq [-\infty, \infty)$  that is unbounded above. We may assume that  $-\infty \notin Q$  and  $1 \notin Q$  (for if not, remove them).

We know that  $D_q(\mathbf{p})$  is continuous in  $q \in [-\infty, \infty]$ , by Lemma 4.2.7 or Lemma 6.2.4(i). Since  $Q$  is unbounded above,

$$
\lim_{q\in Q,q\to \infty}D_{q}(\mathbf{p}) = D_{\infty}(\mathbf{p}) = 1\bigg{/}\max_{1\leq i\leq n}p_{i}.
$$

The same is true for  $D_q(\mathbf{r})$ . Hence by assumption,  $\max_i p_i = \max_i r_i$ . Choose  $k$  and  $\ell$  such that  $p_k = \max_i p_i$  and  $r_\ell = \max_i r_i$ . Then  $p_k = r_\ell$ .

If  $p_k = r_\ell = 1$  then  $\mathbf{p}$  and  $\mathbf{r}$  are both of the form  $(0, \dots, 0, 1, 0, \dots, 0)$ , so one is a permutation of the other. Assuming otherwise, define  $\mathbf{p}', \mathbf{r}' \in \Delta_{n-1}$  by

$$
\mathbf {p} ^ {\prime} = \left(\frac {p _ {1}}{1 - p _ {k}}, \dots , \frac {p _ {k - 1}}{1 - p _ {k}}, \frac {p _ {k + 1}}{1 - p _ {k}}, \dots , \frac {p _ {n}}{1 - p _ {k}}\right)
$$

and similarly for  $\mathbf{r}'$ . Then for all  $q \in Q$

$$
\begin{array}{l} D _ {q} \left(\mathbf {p} ^ {\prime}\right) = (1 - p _ {k}) ^ {q / (q - 1)} \left(\sum_ {i \neq k} p _ {i} ^ {q}\right) ^ {1 / (1 - q)} \\ = (1 - p _ {k}) ^ {q / (q - 1)} \left(D _ {q} (\mathbf {p}) ^ {1 - q} - p _ {k} ^ {q}\right) ^ {1 / (1 - q)}. \\ \end{array}
$$

Similarly,

$$
D _ {q} (\mathbf {r} ^ {\prime}) = (1 - r _ {\ell}) ^ {q / (q - 1)} \bigl (D _ {q} (\mathbf {r}) ^ {1 - q} - r _ {\ell} ^ {q} \bigr) ^ {1 / (1 - q)}.
$$

But  $p_k = r_\ell$  and  $D_q(\mathbf{p}) = D_q(\mathbf{r})$ , so  $D_q(\mathbf{p}') = D_q(\mathbf{r}')$ . This holds for all  $q \in Q$ , so by inductive hypothesis,  $\mathbf{p}'$  is a permutation of  $\mathbf{r}'$ . It follows that  $\mathbf{p}$  is a permutation of  $\mathbf{r}$ , completing the induction.

# A.4 Affine functions

Here we prove Lemma 5.1.7, which is restated here for convenience.

Lemma 5.1.7 Let  $\alpha \colon I\to J$  be a function between real intervals. The following are equivalent:

i.  $\alpha$  is affine;

ii.  $\alpha (\sum \lambda_{i}x_{i}) = \sum \lambda_{i}\alpha (x_{i})$  for all  $n\geq 1$ $x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\in I$  and  $\lambda_1,\dots ,\lambda_n\in \mathbb{R}$  such that  $\sum \lambda_{i} = 1$  and  $\sum \lambda_{i}x_{i}\in I$

iii. there exist constants  $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$  such that  $\alpha(x) = ax + b$  for all  $x \in I$ ;

iv.  $\alpha$  is continuous and  $\alpha\left(\frac{1}{2}(x_1 + x_2)\right) = \frac{1}{2}\left(\alpha(x_1) + \alpha(x_2)\right)$  for all  $x_1, x_2 \in I$ .

Proof First we assume (i) and prove (ii). By induction,

$$
\alpha \left(\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} x _ {i}\right) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} \alpha \left(x _ {i}\right) \tag {A.3}
$$

for all  $n \geq 1$ ,  $\mathbf{p} \in \Delta_n$ , and  $\mathbf{x} \in I^n$ . Now let  $n \geq 1$ ,  $x_1, \ldots, x_n \in I$  and  $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n \in \mathbb{R}$  with  $\sum \lambda_i = 1$  and  $\sum \lambda_i x_i \in I$ . Assume without loss of generality that

$$
\lambda_ {1}, \dots , \lambda_ {k} \geq 0, \quad \lambda_ {k + 1}, \dots , \lambda_ {n} <   0
$$

for some  $k\in \{1,\ldots ,n\}$  .Write

$$
\mu = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \lambda_ {i} = 1 - \sum_ {i = k + 1} ^ {n} \lambda_ {i} \geq 1, \quad w = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \lambda_ {i} x _ {i} \in I.
$$

Then

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \frac {\lambda_ {i}}{\mu} x _ {i} = \frac {1}{\mu} w + \sum_ {i = k + 1} ^ {n} \frac {- \lambda_ {i}}{\mu} x _ {i}.
$$

The coefficients  $\lambda_1 / \mu, \dots, \lambda_k / \mu$  on the left-hand side are nonnegative and sum to 1, and the same is true of the coefficients  $1 / \mu, -\lambda_{k + 1} / \mu, \dots, -\lambda_n / \mu$  on the right-hand side. Hence we can apply  $\alpha$  throughout and use equation (A.3) on both sides, giving

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \frac {\lambda_ {i}}{\mu} \alpha (x _ {i}) = \frac {1}{\mu} \alpha (w) + \sum_ {i = k + 1} ^ {n} \frac {- \lambda_ {i}}{\mu} \alpha (x _ {i}).
$$

Rearranging gives

$$
\alpha (w) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \lambda_ {i} \alpha (x _ {i}),
$$

proving (ii).

Next we assume (ii) and prove (iii). If  $I$  is trivial, the result is trivial. Otherwise, we can choose distinct  $x_{1}, x_{2} \in I$ . Put

$$
a = \frac {\alpha (x _ {2}) - \alpha (x _ {1})}{x _ {2} - x _ {1}}, \qquad b = \frac {\alpha (x _ {1}) x _ {2} - \alpha (x _ {2}) x _ {1}}{x _ {2} - x _ {1}},
$$

and define  $\alpha' \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$  by  $\alpha'(x) = ax + b$ . We show that  $\alpha(x) = \alpha'(x)$  for all  $x \in I$ . First, this is true when  $x \in \{x_1, x_2\}$ , by direct calculation. Second, every element of  $I$  can be written as  $\lambda_1 x_1 + \lambda_2 x_2$  for some  $\lambda_1, \lambda_2 \in \mathbb{R}$  with  $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = 1$ . Since both  $\alpha$  and  $\alpha'$  satisfy (ii), the result follows.

Trivially, (iii) implies (iv).

Finally, assuming (iv), we prove (i). By continuity, it is enough to prove that

$$
\alpha \left(p x _ {1} + (1 - p) x _ {2}\right) = p \alpha \left(x _ {1}\right) + (1 - p) \alpha \left(x _ {2}\right)
$$

whenever  $x_{1}, x_{2} \in I$  and  $p \in [0, 1]$  is a dyadic rational, that is,  $p = m / 2^n$  for some integers  $n \geq 0$  and  $0 \leq m \leq 2^n$ . We do this by induction on  $n$ . It is trivial for  $n = 0$ . Now let  $n \geq 1$  and assume the result for  $n - 1$ . Let  $x_{1}, x_{2} \in I$ , let  $0 \leq m \leq 2^n$ , and assume without loss of generality that  $m \leq 2^{n - 1}$  (otherwise we can reverse the roles of  $x_{1}$  and  $x_{2}$ ). Then

$$
\begin{array}{l} \alpha \left(\frac {m}{2 ^ {n}} x _ {1} + \left(1 - \frac {m}{2 ^ {n}}\right) x _ {2}\right) = \alpha \left(\frac {m}{2 ^ {n - 1}} \cdot \frac {1}{2} \left(x _ {1} + x _ {2}\right) + \left(1 - \frac {m}{2 ^ {n - 1}}\right) x _ {2}\right) (A.4) \\ = \frac {m}{2 ^ {n - 1}} \alpha \left(\frac {1}{2} \left(x _ {1} + x _ {2}\right)\right) + \left(1 - \frac {m}{2 ^ {n - 1}}\right) \alpha \left(x _ {2}\right) (A.5) \\ = \frac {m}{2 ^ {n - 1}} \cdot \frac {1}{2} (\alpha (x _ {1}) + \alpha (x _ {2})) + \left(1 - \frac {m}{2 ^ {n - 1}}\right) \alpha (x _ {2}) (A.6) \\ = \frac {m}{2 ^ {n}} \alpha \left(x _ {1}\right) + \left(1 - \frac {m}{2 ^ {n}}\right) \alpha \left(x _ {2}\right), (A.7) \\ \end{array}
$$

where (A.4) and (A.7) are elementary, (A.5) is by inductive hypothesis, and (A.6) is by (iv). This completes the induction and, therefore, the proof.  $\square$

# A.5 Diversity of integer orders

Here we prove the statement made in Example 6.1.7 on computation of the diversity  $D_q^Z(\mathbf{p})$  for integers  $q \geq 2$ : that in the notation defined there,

$$
D _ {q} ^ {Z} (\mathbf {p}) = \mu_ {q} ^ {1 / (1 - q)}.
$$

Indeed, adopting the convention that all sums run over  $1,\ldots ,n$

$$
\begin{array}{l} D _ {q} ^ {Z} (\mathbf {p}) ^ {1 - q} = \sum_ {i} p _ {i} \left(\sum_ {j} Z _ {i j} p _ {j}\right) ^ {q - 1} \\ = \sum_ {i, j _ {1}, \dots , j _ {q - 1}} p _ {i} Z _ {i j _ {1}} p _ {j _ {1}} Z _ {i j _ {2}} p _ {j _ {2}} \dots Z _ {i j _ {q - 1}} p _ {j _ {q - 1}} \\ = \sum_ {i _ {1}, i _ {2}, \dots , i _ {q}} p _ {i _ {1}} p _ {i _ {2}} \dots p _ {i _ {q}} Z _ {i _ {1} i _ {2}} Z _ {i _ {1} i _ {3}} \dots Z _ {i _ {1} i _ {q}} \\ \mathbf {\mu} = \mu_ {q}, \\ \end{array}
$$

as required.

# A.6 The maximum entropy of a coupling

Let  $\mathbf{p}$  and  $\mathbf{r}$  be probability distributions on finite sets  $X$  and  $\mathcal{Y}$ , respectively. We showed in Remark 8.1.13 that among all distributions on  $X \times \mathcal{Y}$  with marginals  $\mathbf{p}$  and  $\mathbf{r}$ , none has greater entropy than  $\mathbf{p} \otimes \mathbf{r}$ . In other words,

$$
H (P) \leq H (\mathbf {p} \otimes \mathbf {r}) \tag {A.8}
$$

for all probability distributions  $P$  on  $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$  whose marginal distributions are  $\mathbf{p}$  and  $\mathbf{r}$ . It was also claimed there that unless  $q = 0$  or  $q = 1$ , the inequality (A.8) fails when  $H$  is replaced by the Rényi entropy  $H_{q}$  or the  $q$ -logarithmic entropy  $S_{q}$ . Here we prove this claim.

Since  $H_{q}$  and  $S_{q}$  are increasing, invertible transformations of one another, it suffices to prove it for  $H_{q}$ . And since Rényi entropy is logarithmic (equation (4.14)), the inequality in question can be restated as

$$
H _ {q} (P) \leq H _ {q} (\mathbf {p}) + H _ {q} (\mathbf {r}). \tag {A.9}
$$

This is true for  $q = 0$ :

$$
\operatorname {s u p p} (P) \subseteq \operatorname {s u p p} (\mathbf {p}) \times \operatorname {s u p p} (\mathbf {r}),
$$

so

$$
| \operatorname {s u p p} (P) | \leq | \operatorname {s u p p} (\mathbf {p}) | \cdot | \operatorname {s u p p} (\mathbf {r}) |,
$$

giving

$$
H _ {0} (P) = \log | \operatorname {s u p p} (P) | \leq \log | \operatorname {s u p p} (\mathbf {p}) | + \log | \operatorname {s u p p} (\mathbf {r}) | = H _ {0} (\mathbf {p}) + H _ {0} (\mathbf {r}).
$$

Our task now is to show that except in the cases  $q = 0$  and  $q = 1$ , the inequality (A.9) is false. Thus, we prove that for each  $q \in (0,1) \cup (1,\infty]$ , there exist

finite sets  $X$  and  $\mathcal{Y}$  and a probability distribution  $P$  on  $X\times \mathcal{Y}$  such that

$$
H _ {q} (P) > H _ {q} (\mathbf {p}) + H _ {q} (\mathbf {r}),
$$

where  $\mathbf{p}$  and  $\mathbf{r}$  are the marginal distributions of  $P$ .

We will treat separately the cases  $q \in (0,1)$ ,  $q \in (1,\infty)$ , and  $q = \infty$ . In all cases, we will take  $\mathcal{X} = \mathcal{Y} = \{1,\dots,N\}$  for some  $N$ . A probability distribution  $P$  on  $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$  is then an  $N \times N$  matrix of nonnegative real numbers whose entries sum to 1, and its marginals  $\mathbf{p}$  and  $\mathbf{r}$  are given by the row-sums and column-sums:

$$
p _ {i} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {N} P _ {i j}, \qquad r _ {j} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} P _ {i j}
$$

$(i,j\in \{1,\dots ,N\})$

First let  $q \in (0,1)$ . For each  $N \geq 2$ , define an  $N \times N$  matrix  $P$  by

$$
P = \left( \begin{array}{c c c c} 1 - (N - 1) ^ {(q - 1) / q} & 0 & \dots & 0 \\ 0 & (N - 1) ^ {(- q - 1) / q} & \dots & (N - 1) ^ {(- q - 1) / q} \\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ 0 & (N - 1) ^ {(- q - 1) / q} & \dots & (N - 1) ^ {(- q - 1) / q} \end{array} \right).
$$

The entries of  $P$  sum to 1, and  $1 - (N - 1)^{(q - 1) / q} \geq 0$  since  $q \in (0,1)$ , so  $P \in \Delta_{N^2}$ . We have

$$
\begin{array}{l} H _ {q} (P) = \frac {1}{1 - q} \log \left(\left(1 - (N - 1) ^ {(q - 1) / q}\right) ^ {q} + (N - 1) ^ {2} (N - 1) ^ {- q - 1}\right) \\ \geq \frac {1}{1 - q} \log ((N - 1) ^ {- q + 1}) \\ = \log (N - 1). \\ \end{array}
$$

The marginals of  $P$  are

$$
\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r} = \Big(1 - (N - 1)^{(q - 1) / q},\underbrace{(N - 1)^{-1 / q},\ldots,(N - 1)^{-1 / q}}_{N - 1}\Big),
$$

so

$$
\begin{array}{l} H _ {q} (\mathbf {p}) = H _ {q} (\mathbf {r}) = \frac {1}{1 - q} \log \left(\left(1 - (N - 1) ^ {(q - 1) / q}\right) ^ {q} + (N - 1) \cdot (N - 1) ^ {- 1}\right) \\ <   \frac {1}{1 - q} \log 2. \\ \end{array}
$$

Hence

$$
H _ {q} (P) - \left(H _ {q} (\mathbf {p}) + H _ {q} (\mathbf {r})\right) > \log (N - 1) - \frac {2}{1 - q} \log 2 \rightarrow \infty
$$

as  $N\to \infty$  . In particular,  $H_{q}(P) > H_{q}(\mathbf{p}) + H_{q}(\mathbf{r})$  when  $N$  is sufficiently large.

Now let  $q \in (1, \infty)$ . For each  $N \geq 2$ , define an  $N \times N$  matrix  $P$  by

$$
P = \left( \begin{array}{c c c c} 0 & 1 / 2 (N - 1) & \dots & 1 / 2 (N - 1) \\ 1 / 2 (N - 1) & 0 & \dots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ 1 / 2 (N - 1) & 0 & \dots & 0 \end{array} \right).
$$

The entries of  $P$  are nonnegative and sum to 1, and

$$
H _ {q} (P) = H _ {q} \left(\mathbf {u} _ {2 (N - 1)}\right) = \log (2 (N - 1)) \rightarrow \infty
$$

as  $N\to \infty$  . The marginals of  $P$  are

$$
\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r} = (1 / 2,\underbrace{1 / 2(N - 1),\ldots,1 / 2(N - 1)}_{N - 1}),
$$

and

$$
\begin{array}{l} H _ {q} (\mathbf {p}) = H _ {q} (\mathbf {r}) = \frac {1}{1 - q} \log \left(\left(1 / 2\right) ^ {q} + (N - 1) \cdot \left(1 / 2 (N - 1)\right) ^ {q}\right) \\ = \frac {1}{1 - q} \log ((1 / 2) ^ {q}) + \frac {1}{1 - q} \log (1 + (N - 1) ^ {1 - q}) \\ \rightarrow \frac {1}{1 - q} \log ((1 / 2) ^ {q}) \\ \end{array}
$$

as  $N\to \infty$  , since  $q > 1$  . Hence

$$
H _ {q} (P) - \left(H _ {q} (\mathbf {p}) + H _ {q} (\mathbf {r})\right)\rightarrow \infty
$$

as  $N \to \infty$ , which again implies that  $H_{q}(P) > H_{q}(\mathbf{p}) + H_{q}(\mathbf{r})$  when  $N$  is sufficiently large.

Finally, let  $q = \infty$ . The same matrix  $P$  as in the previous case has

$$
\begin{array}{l} H _ {\infty} (P) = \log (2 (N - 1)), \\ H _ {\infty} (\mathbf {p}) = H _ {\infty} (\mathbf {r}) = \log 2. \\ \end{array}
$$

Hence

$$
H _ {\infty} (P) - \left(H _ {\infty} (\mathbf {p}) + H _ {\infty} (\mathbf {r})\right) = \log (2 (N - 1)) - 2 \log 2 \rightarrow \infty
$$

as  $N \to \infty$ . Once again, this implies that  $H_{\infty}(P) > H_{\infty}(\mathbf{p}) + H_{\infty}(\mathbf{r})$  for sufficiently large  $N$ .

# A.7 Convex duality

Here we prove Theorem 9.2.7, which is restated here for convenience.

Theorem 9.2.7 (Legendre-Fenchel) Let  $f\colon \mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}$  be a convex function. Then  $f^{**} = f$ .

Proof Let  $x \in \mathbb{R}$ . By definition of convex conjugate,

$$
\begin{array}{l} f ^ {* *} (x) = \sup  _ {\lambda \in \mathbb {R}} \left(\lambda x - f ^ {*} (\lambda)\right) \\ = \sup  _ {\lambda \in \mathbb {R}} \inf  _ {y \in \mathbb {R}} (\lambda (x - y) + f (y)). \tag {A.10} \\ \end{array}
$$

In particular,

$$
f^{**}(x)\leq \sup_{\lambda \in \mathbb{R}}\bigl(\lambda (x - x) + f(x)\bigr) = f(x),
$$

so it remains to prove that  $f^{**}(x) \geq f(x)$ . In fact, we will show that there exists  $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$  such that

$$
\lambda (x - y) + f (y) \geq f (x) \text {f o r a l l} y \in \mathbb {R}. \tag {A.11}
$$

By (A.10), this will suffice. Now, a real number  $\lambda$  satisfies (A.11) if and only if

$$
\sup  _ {y \in (- \infty , x)} \frac {f (x) - f (y)}{x - y} \leq \lambda \leq \inf  _ {z \in (x, \infty)} \frac {f (z) - f (x)}{z - x},
$$

so such a  $\lambda$  exists if and only if

$$
\frac {f (x) - f (y)}{x - y} \leq \frac {f (z) - f (x)}{z - x} \tag {A.12}
$$

for all  $y < x < z$ . We now prove this. Take  $y$  and  $z$  such that  $y < x < z$ . Then  $x = py + (1 - p)z$  for some  $p \in (0,1)$ , and the inequality (A.12) to be proved states that

$$
\frac {f (x) - f (y)}{(1 - p) (z - y)} \leq \frac {f (z) - f (x)}{p (z - y)},
$$

or equivalently,

$$
f (x) \leq p f (y) + (1 - p) f (z).
$$

This is true by convexity of  $f$ .

# A.8 Cumulant generating functions are convex

In Section 9.2, we used the fact that the cumulant generating function of any real random variable is convex. Here we prove this.

If we are willing to assume that the cumulant generating function is twice differentiable, then the result can be deduced from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, as in Section 5.11 of Grimmett and Stirzaker [128]. But there is no need to make this assumption. Instead, we use a more general standard inequality:

Theorem A.8.1 (Hölder's inequality) Let  $\Omega$  be a measure space, let  $p, q \in (1, \infty)$  with  $1/p + 1/q = 1$ , and let  $f, g: \Omega \to [0, \infty)$  be measurable functions. Then

$$
\int_ {\Omega} f g \leq \left(\int_ {\Omega} f ^ {p}\right) ^ {1 / p} \left(\int_ {\Omega} g ^ {q}\right) ^ {1 / q}.
$$

Here we allow the possibility that one or more of the integrals is  $\infty$ .

Proof This is Theorem 6.2 of Folland [106], for instance.

![](images/c0c5b2eddf3f885bad1e44b1b7f0001182736cbb48585f8e4418bce0c37a97b1.jpg)

Corollary A.8.2 Let  $X$  be a real random variable. Then the function

$$
\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{c c c}\mathbb {R}&\rightarrow&[ 0, \infty ]\end{array} \\ \lambda \mapsto \log \mathbb {E} \left(e ^ {\lambda X}\right) \\ \end{array}
$$

is convex.

Proof We have to prove that for all  $\lambda, \mu \in \mathbb{R}$  and  $t \in [0,1]$ ,

$$
\log \mathbb {E} \left(e ^ {(t \lambda + (1 - t) \mu) X}\right) \leq t \log \mathbb {E} \left(e ^ {\lambda X}\right) + (1 - t) \log \mathbb {E} \left(e ^ {\mu X}\right),
$$

or equivalently,

$$
\mathbb {E} \left(e ^ {t \lambda X} e ^ {(1 - t) \mu X}\right) \leq \mathbb {E} \left(e ^ {\lambda X}\right) ^ {t} \mathbb {E} \left(e ^ {\mu X}\right) ^ {1 - t}.
$$

This is trivial if  $t = 0$  or  $t = 1$ . Supposing otherwise, write  $p = 1 / t$ ,  $q = 1 / (1 - t)$ ,  $U = e^{t.\lambda X}$ , and  $V = e^{(1 - t)\mu X}$ . Thus,  $p, q \in (1,\infty)$  with  $1 / p + 1 / q = 1$ , and  $U$  and  $V$  are nonnegative real random variables on the same sample space. The inequality to be proved is that

$$
\mathbb {E} (U V) \leq \mathbb {E} (U ^ {p}) ^ {1 / p} \mathbb {E} (V ^ {q}) ^ {1 / q},
$$

which is just Hölder's inequality in probabilistic notation.

![](images/e38b7ae120b28059ea840983c34f9f4c7bc118c704d49a5beb3b292e83540468.jpg)

# A.9 Functions on a finite field

Here we prove Lemma 11.4.1, which is restated here for convenience.

Lemma 11.4.1 Let  $K$  be a finite field with  $q$  elements, let  $n \geq 0$ , and let  $F \colon K^n \to K$  be a function. Then there is a unique polynomial  $f$  of the form

$$
f \left(x _ {1}, \dots , x _ {n}\right) = \sum_ {0 \leq r _ {1}, \dots , r _ {n} <   q} c _ {r _ {1}, \dots , r _ {n}} x _ {1} ^ {r _ {1}} \dots x _ {n} ^ {r _ {n}} \tag {A.13}
$$

$(c_{r_1,\ldots ,r_n}\in K)$  such that

$$
f \left(\pi_ {1}, \dots , \pi_ {n}\right) = F \left(\pi_ {1}, \dots , \pi_ {n}\right)
$$

for all  $\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_n \in K$ .

This result is standard. For instance, Section 10.3 of Roman [297] gives a proof in the case  $n = 1$ .

Proof Write  $K^{<q}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$  for the set of polynomials of degree less than  $q$  in each variable, that is, of the form (A.13). Write  $R(f): K^n \to K$  for the function induced by a polynomial  $f$  in  $n$  variables. Then  $R$  defines a map

$$
R \colon K ^ {<   q} [ x _ {1}, \dots , x _ {n} ] \to \{\text {f u n c t i o n s} K ^ {n} \rightarrow K \}.
$$

We have to prove that  $R$  is bijective. Both domain and codomain have  $q^{q^n}$  elements, so it suffices to prove that  $R$  is surjective.

First define a polynomial  $\delta$  by

$$
\delta (x _ {1}, \ldots , x _ {n}) = (1 - x _ {1} ^ {q - 1}) \dots (1 - x _ {n} ^ {q - 1}).
$$

Then  $\delta$  has degree  $q - 1$  in each variable, and for  $a_1,\ldots ,a_n\in K$

$$
R (\delta) (a _ {1}, \ldots , a _ {n}) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \text {i f} a _ {1} = \dots = a _ {n} = 0, \\ 0 & \text {o t h e r w i s e .} \end{array} \right.
$$

Now, given a function  $F \colon K^n \to K$ , define a polynomial  $f$  by

$$
f \left(x _ {1}, \dots , x _ {n}\right) = \sum_ {a _ {1}, \dots , a _ {n} \in K} F \left(a _ {1}, \dots , a _ {n}\right) \delta \left(x _ {1} - a _ {1}, \dots , x _ {n} - a _ {n}\right).
$$

Then  $f$  has degree at most  $q - 1$  in each variable and  $R(f) = F$ , as required.

There are other proofs. For instance, one can prove that  $R$  is injective rather than surjective, showing by induction on  $n$  that its kernel is trivial. I thank Todd Trimble for pointing out to me the Lagrange interpolation argument above.

# Diversity measures

The following conditions apply to a sequence  $(D\colon \Delta_n\to (0,\infty))_{n\geq 1}$  of functions, that is, a diversity measure for communities modelled as finite probability distributions (without incorporating species similarity).

<table><tr><td>Name</td><td>Abbreviated definition</td><td>Reference</td></tr><tr><td>Absence-invariant</td><td>D(.,pi-1,0,pi+1,.) = D(.,pi-1,pi+1,.)</td><td>Def 4.4.7</td></tr><tr><td>Continuous</td><td>D: Δn→(0,∞) is continuous</td><td>Def 4.4.5</td></tr><tr><td>Continuous in positive probabilities</td><td>D: Δ°n→(0,∞) is continuous</td><td>Def 4.4.5</td></tr><tr><td>Effective number</td><td>D(u_n) = n</td><td>Def 2.4.5</td></tr><tr><td>Modular</td><td>D(w○(p^1,.,p^n)) depends only on w and D(p^1),.,.,D(p^n)</td><td>p. 56, Def 4.4.14</td></tr><tr><td>Modular-monotone</td><td>D(p^i) ≤ D(¯p^i) for all i ⇒ D(w○(p^1,.,p^n)) ≤ D(w○(¯p^1,.,.,¯p^n))</td><td>Def 7.4.1</td></tr><tr><td>Multiplicative</td><td>D(p⊗r) = D(p)D(r)</td><td>Def 4.4.16</td></tr><tr><td>Normalized</td><td>D(u_1) = 1</td><td>p. 246</td></tr><tr><td>Replication principle</td><td>D(u_n⊗p) = nD(p)</td><td>p. 56, Def 4.4.18</td></tr><tr><td>Symmetric</td><td>D(p) = D(pσ)</td><td>p. 96</td></tr></table>

# Value measures

The following conditions apply to a sequence  $(\sigma \colon \Delta_n \times (0, \infty)^n \to (0, \infty))_{n \geq 1}$  of functions. Such a sequence is of the same type as a weighted mean on  $(0, \infty)$ , and the same terminology applies. We also use two further conditions.

<table><tr><td>Name</td><td>Abbreviated definition</td><td>Reference</td></tr><tr><td>Continuous in positive probabilities</td><td>σ(−, v): Δn° → (0,∞) is continuous</td><td>Def 7.3.1</td></tr><tr><td>Effective number</td><td>σ(u_n, (1, ..., 1)) = n</td><td>Def 7.3.2</td></tr></table>
